findings.verdict_notes: The file is 11k lines with many responsibilities. The separable identity-reconcile section is plausible, and the lock use at 5955 and 10166 shows the reach-back coupling. The 383 private-touch test count was not re-counted, but the structural claim stands.

findings.title: cross_graph_move recreates RELATES_TO edges without expired_at (and the merge audit stamps), stripping the restored-edge signature on every cross-graph move
findings.statement: move_entity_across_graphs, both arms of _recreate_subgraph_relationships_batch, and merge_foreign_duplicate all read edges with `RETURN e.uuid, e.name, e.fact, e.valid_at, e.invalid_at, e.created_at, e.group_id, e.episodes, s.uuid, t.uuid`. They recreate the edge with a SET list of uuid, name, fact, valid_at, invalid_at, created_at, group_id, episodes and fact_embedding. expired_at, superseded_edge_uuid and reassigned_from_node_uuid are neither read nor written. GraphitiBackend.redirect_node_edges' own docstring (task 4986) says expired_at SET with invalid_at NULL is the restore hooks' deliberately-restored signature, and that dropping it 're-exposes a restored edge to false supersession'. Every restored edge moved by migrate_cross_graph_leak or consolidate_namespace_families therefore silently loses that protection and its merge audit trail. This is the same omission 4986 fixed in redirect_node_edges.
findings.proposal: Add e.expired_at, e.superseded_edge_uuid and e.reassigned_from_node_uuid to the RETURN tuple and the SET list at all four recreate sites. Add a regression test that moves a node carrying an edge with invalid_at NULL and expired_at set, and asserts both values and the audit stamps survive in the target graph. The structural fix (one generated property list) is the edge-lifecycle finding.
findings.bug_history_link: Same omission class as d9cdb80a68 fix(4986) 'redirect_node_edges preserves expired_at'; cross-graph-move sites last reworked by 2451 (de24658515, eaa5fc4d27, 576ba7e0cd, fe277b8a68, c739680767, cac999435f), none of which added expired_at
findings.verdict_notes: grep finds zero occurrences of expired_at in cross_graph_move.py, and its SET lists (lines about 700, 754, 1215, 1297, 1463, 1908) lack it. graphiti_client.py redirect_node_edges explicitly preserves expired_at (task 4986 docstring at about 2900). The omission is real.

findings.title: Merge-lane, scheduler and worktree operations live inside the escalation server and reach back into orchestrator through function-local imports
findings.statement: Heuristic 14 measurement. create_server (server.py lines 912-5232, about 4,300 lines) is one closure. An AST pass over its 35 nested functions partitions them by which captured inputs they use. Group A, lines about 1000-3520, holds the escalation tools and their helpers (filing chokepoint, resolve_issue, promote_to_l2, stamp/declare_pin/amend, reads); every function in it closes over `queue` only (plus the two status/claimant lookups, and harness for a pins annotation). Group B, lines 3524-5232 (about 1,700 lines), holds merge_request (815 lines, 194-line docstring, 26 decision nodes), merge_status, merge_cancel, _durable_terminal_state, release_workflow, halt/unhalt_merge_queue, get_merge_queue, get_task_runtime_state, halt/resume_scheduler, reload_config, claim/release_warm_worktree. Every one of these closes over harness, event_store, merge_queue, orch_config or merge_inflight_registry, and none uses `queue`. Heuristic-13 symptoms are measurable: server.py carries 10 function-local `from orchestrator... import` statements, each with `# type: ignore[reportMissingImports]` (orchestrator.merge_queue x4, landing_evidence, merge_lane, event_store, git_ops x2 including the private git_ops._run); git_authority.py and merge_lane_resolution.py add 2 each (14 in total). escalation/pyproject.toml declares orchestrator only as a dev dependency, while orchestrator/pyproject.toml depends on escalation and 133 orchestrator import sites import escalation. git_authority.py's own docstring states the imports resolve 'only because the escalation server is hosted inside the orchestrator process'. The lower layer therefore imports the upper one at runtime, and harness is duck-typed Any (_get_merge_worker, hasattr(worker,'snapshot'), getattr on harness). Layer-direction constants have to be copied and pinned by tests (authority.py _WATCHER_AUTO_IDENTITY and PROMOTE_SENTINEL_BOUND_ROLES). Group B is where the fix history sits: task 3103 (6 commits: ancestor arm, marker arm, degenerate-branch guards), 2945, 2927, 2928, 3724, 4887, 4888.
findings.proposal: Move Group B into orchestrator as `orchestrator/src/orchestrator/mcp/lane_tools.py::register_lane_tools(mcp, harness, merge_queue, event_store, orch_config, inflight_registry)`, called by harness.py right after `escalation.server.create_server(...)` returns the FastMCP instance. Tool names (mcp__escalation__merge_request and the rest) are unchanged because they register on the same server object. Move git_authority.py and merge_lane_resolution.py with them; the landed reconciler (η) already imports git_authority statically from orchestrator. `merge_inflight_registry`, `_waiters`, `_get_merge_worker` and `_get_terminal_retention` move with the tools, so merge_request, merge_status and merge_cancel stay together. Inside orchestrator these become static downward imports and typed harness/MergeWorker parameters. Code that dies: all 14 function-local orchestrator imports and their pyright ignores, the duck-typed getattr/hasattr probes of harness, the 'escalation standalone' None branches in each ops tool, the dev-dependency cycle in escalation/pyproject.toml, and the reverse-import pins in tests/test_authority.py for constants that can then be imported from their owner. Escalation's create_server shrinks to Group A (about 2,500 lines, still to be split under finding 'resolve_issue / promote_to_l2 / chokepoint gate chains'). This would have prevented the 'merge-lane bugs patched in the escalation package' class (3103 series, 2927, 2928).
findings.bug_history_link: 3103 series (fix(3103): guard merge_status's ancestor/marker arm, decline already_merged fast-path for a degenerate branch); 2945 patch-id already-merged backstop; 2927 duplicate_in_verify; 2928 merge_cancel retirement; 3724 release_workflow orphan park; 4887 'create git_authority.py' extraction; refactor(5036) 'delete the re-export shims and reach-back imports'; 27 of 132 window commits on server.py concern merge/worktree/release tools
findings.verdict_notes: Counted function-local `from orchestrator...` imports in server.py::create_server, each with `# type: ignore[reportMissingImports]`. The git_authority.py docstring says the import resolves only because the server is hosted inside the orchestrator process. escalation/pyproject.toml lists orchestrator as dev-only and orchestrator/pyproject.toml depends on escalation. I did not recount the 35 nested functions or the group A/B partition.

findings.title: Record identity changes with lifecycle state (file moves root to archive), so every reader re-implements locate, retry and vanish handling and every writer re-implements the locked pending-only RMW
findings.statement: Resolving a record writes it to queue_dir/{id}.json and then os.replace's it into archive/YYYY-MM-DD/, so the path of a record is its lifecycle state. Consequences measured in queue.py (3,473 lines, 12/81 fix commits): (a) locating an id needs a memoised per-subdir listing, a cross-process re-probe, a negative cache with a hard cap and wholesale clearing (_locate_path, _cache_archive_negative, _archive_listing, _archive_negative_cache); (b) get() needs a 2-attempt re-locate loop for the move race (5118); (c) there are four separate root-then-archive scans, each with its own seen-set precedence rule (get_by_task, iter_all_escalation_paths, _scan_archive_listing, sweep.sweep) plus a tri-state read helper (read_escalation_for_scan, #5111) that all of them must remember to use; (d) the pending-only locked RMW is hand-copied at 8 sites: grep finds `Escalation.from_json(path.read_text())` under `escalation_id_lock` in add_members_to_l2, stamp_triage, amend, declare_pin, attach_dedupe_child, patch_resolution_metadata and note_suppressed_refile, with the same 'queue root only, never self.get(), or _rewrite resurrects an archived record' comment re-explained in each. The per-id sidecar locks add their own lifecycle (8,901 then 9,461 stale .json.lock dirents, reaped by sweep.reap_orphan_locks). The storage primitives (lock, scan, tri-state read, archive layout) are defined inside the 3,473-line queue.py and imported upward from it by sweep.py, watcher.py and shadow_ruling.py (and by the dashboard's iter_all_escalation_paths). Tests pin the cache internals (`q._archive_listing`, `_archive_negative_cache`, `_iter_archive_paths`, `queue._rewrite`: about 12 reach-ins), the interface-smell stance.
findings.proposal: Extract `escalation/src/escalation/store.py::RecordStore`, the single owner of the on-disk layout. It would expose `read(id) -> Record | Absent | Unreadable` (a typed tri-state), `scan(status) -> Iterator[Record]` (one two-tier iterator with the seen-set rule and the vanished/unreadable channel built in), `mutate_pending(id, fn) -> MutateResult` (lock, root-only read, pending guard, apply fn, atomic write, all in one place) and `archive(id)`. Queue lifecycle logic (resolve, park, dedupe, L2 membership) then becomes pure policy over RecordStore; sweep, watcher, shadow_ruling and the dashboard import the lower layer, not queue.py. Code that dies: the seven hand-copied lock/read/guard blocks, the get() retry loop, the memo and negative-cache pair (or they become private to RecordStore and untested from outside), the duplicated scan loops, and the Defect-2 resurrection comments. A longer-term alternative is to stop moving files on resolve (status lives in the file, archiving becomes a quiescent retention pass), which removes the move race by construction. Bug classes prevented: vanishing pending L2s (2846), mid-scan relocation (#5111), get TOCTOU (5118), patch_resolution_metadata without the lock (4552), resurrection of archived records.
findings.bug_history_link: #5111 series (survive a mid-scan archival in get_by_task; add the loud 'unreadable' channel; survive mid-scan relocation in sweep); 5118 get() TOCTOU retry; 4552 patch_resolution_metadata takes the per-id lock; 2846 submit() writes the pending record durably; 2810 targeted archive re-probe on memo miss; 4566 8,901 .json.lock dirents; 99d6e06af1 fix(5649) escalation_id_lock re-validates its inode after flock; 4132/4335 attach_dedupe_child updated_at and children bound
findings.verdict_notes: Root-then-archive layout and the multiple scans are real. sweep.py, watcher.py and shadow_ruling.py import escalation_id_lock, read_escalation_for_scan and iter_all_escalation_paths from queue.py. escalation_id_lock appears 37 times in queue.py. A grep for `Escalation.from_json(path.read_text())` finds 7 sites versus the claimed 8, which is minor. 37 test reach-ins to the archive cache internals and `_rewrite`.

findings.title: resolve_issue pre-stamps resolution_action by rewriting a stale snapshot outside the per-id lock, via a private queue method
findings.statement: In resolve_issue, `rec = queue.get(escalation_id)` is read with no lock at the top of the gate sequence. The declared-pin gate then does a further queue.get per cluster member, and only after that does the code run `if rec.status == 'pending': rec.resolution_action = action; queue._rewrite(escalation_id, rec)`. _rewrite is an unlocked whole-record atomic write to the queue ROOT, and this is its only caller outside queue.py (grep: server.py line about 2452; every other _rewrite call is inside an escalation_id_lock block and loads root-only). Two failures follow. (1) If a concurrent resolver or sweep (harness revalidation, orphan reaper, dismiss_all_pending) archives the record between the get and the _rewrite, the rewrite writes a stale status='pending' copy back into the queue root, resurrecting a closed record. The following queue.resolve then finds a root-pending copy, resolves it again, fires _resolve_callback a second time (harness may restart or abandon the task twice) and leaves multi-date archive duplicates; the 4495 late-resolution capture, which exists for exactly this race, is bypassed. (2) A concurrent add_members_to_l2, attach_dedupe_child, amend or declare_pin committed after the snapshot is overwritten by the stale copy (lost members on an L2 about to cascade). The queue's own stamp_triage and amend docstrings name this resurrection hazard; the server path is the one place that ignores it. It also reaches into a private method, which tests mirror.
findings.proposal: Give `EscalationQueue.resolve` a `resolution_action: str | None` parameter and set the field inside the existing locked critical section (queue.park already stamps its own action internally). Delete the pre-stamp block and the `queue._rewrite` call from server.py, and make _rewrite private to the store (see the RecordStore finding). Add a regression test that archives the record between get and resolve and asserts a single resolve callback and no root copy.
findings.bug_history_link: Same class as 4495 (late resolution after a sweep close), 4552 (patch_resolution_metadata took no lock), 1498 'Defect-2' resurrection, 2846; resolution_action pre-stamp came with the C1 action work
findings.verdict_notes: In resolve_issue, `queue._rewrite(escalation_id, rec)` at server.py ~2452 writes the `rec` fetched earlier with no escalation_id_lock. Its own comment says `rec` is reused instead of re-read. `_rewrite` is an unlocked atomic write to the queue root (queue.py::EscalationQueue._rewrite), and server.py is its only caller outside queue.py. The `status == 'pending'` guard runs on the stale snapshot, so the resurrection and lost-update race exists as described.

findings.title: Category, role and severity routing runs on open string vocabularies copied across layers; the one declared enum (CATEGORIES) is dead
findings.statement: Escalation.status, severity, category, agent_role and resolution_action are bare `str` on a roughly 50-field mutable dataclass, with no __post_init__ validation. Measured: (1) server.py::CATEGORIES has 14 entries and no reader outside one test and prose; it lacks milestone_gate, milestone_check_failed, curator_adjudication_missing, mcp_markup_storm, recon_missing_index and about 25 other categories grep finds filed with `category='...'` in orchestrator and fused-memory. models.py carries a comment, 'REFACTOR TRIGGER (task 3709): the NEXT category addition promotes this comment to an enum', and several categories have been added since without doing so. (2) Policy keys on those literals in three places that can drift: authority.py::L2_AUTO_CLOSE_DENY_CATEGORIES (four literals, three duplicated from orchestrator.deterministic_runner constants, 'design_concern' from a bare literal at several call sites), shadow_ruling.py's gate set, and harness revalidation allowlists. (3) Role classification is by prefix: `_HARNESS_SENTINEL_ROLE_PREFIXES = ('harness-', 'orchestrator-')` is defined twice (server.py and submit.py, 'update this tuple whenever server.py's changes') and relied on by orchestrator/lane_lifecycle.py, and its justification is a comment claiming no LLM role uses either prefix. (4) The 'born at L2' fact is level==2 and severity in {critical, urgent} and a sentinel role; it is enforced only by each producer 'by construction' (server.py::_MARKUP_RESIDUE_SEVERITY comment says two sites 'honour the rule by construction rather than by being checked'), while readers fail safe independently (pins.py link 3b treats level 0 + born-at-L2 severity as 'CONTRADICTORY state'; workflow.py treats the two signals as one). (5) The 'downgraded' marker is appended into `summary` ('[downgraded:critical]') and read back by the dedupe key's 3-token slice; the comment admits a known miss for short summaries.
findings.proposal: Introduce `escalation/models.py` enums (`Status`, `Severity`, `Category` as a StrEnum with an `OTHER`/unknown policy, `SentinelRole` via `is_sentinel(role)`), and validate in `Escalation.__post_init__`/`from_dict` so a bad value fails loudly (INV-2) at construction and again at `EscalationQueue.submit`. At submit enforce the single invariant `born_at_l2(severity) <=> level == 2 and is_sentinel(agent_role)` (one definition in models, called from the chokepoint, the CLI and the direct queue.submit sinks). Replace the summary suffix marker with a structured `downgraded_from: str | None` field. Authority's deny set and shadow_ruling's gate set import the Category members. Code that dies: server.CATEGORIES and its test, the duplicated prefix tuple in submit.py, the fail-safe reinterpretations in pins.py link 3b, the lockstep tests for duplicated category literals, and the summary-suffix special case in dedupe keying.
findings.bug_history_link: 3709 (category vocabulary refactor trigger), 3976 severity inflation (severity ordering moved to models), 4541 sentinel-only cluster minted under a real task id, 3690 residue record states its own kind, 4102 curator_adjudication_missing auto-close denial, 2630/4192 auto-close class hardening
findings.verdict_notes: server.py::CATEGORIES has 14 entries and omits milestone_gate and others. action_effects.py calls it inert/unvalidated. models.py has the 'REFACTOR TRIGGER (task 3709)' comment. _HARNESS_SENTINEL_ROLE_PREFIXES is duplicated in server.py and submit.py, with a comment saying to keep them in sync. authority.py::L2_AUTO_CLOSE_DENY_CATEGORIES holds the policy literals.

findings.title: Who may do what is decided inline in 2 of about 30 tools, with a different mechanism each time; ops tools and L2 auto-close lean on other subsystems and on regexes over agent prose
findings.statement: This extends, and does not re-report, escalation.2 and escalation.3 (identified-caller ceilings; header-less callers remain open). New measurements: server.py reads the identity/levels headers at four hand-written sites with four different meanings: resolve_issue parses X-Escalation-Levels and intersects it with a role ceiling; promote_to_l2 checks only identity against PROMOTE_ALLOWED and never consults the levels header (so a levels-capped, identity-less connection can mint L2s); stamp_triage and amend_escalation use the header only for attribution; declare_pin is ungated. The 12 operator tools (halt/resume_scheduler, reload_config, halt/unhalt_merge_queue, release_workflow, merge_cancel, release_warm_worktree and others) have no server-side authorisation at all; their docstrings assert 'appears in no agent role's allow-list', i.e. the guarantee is held by orchestrator's role tool lists, a different subsystem, and shadow_ruling.HUMAN_FOREVER_GATES names 'post_breaker_resume_scheduler' as human-only while resume_scheduler checks nothing. The one place that does gate L2 closes by evidence (authority.py::l2_auto_close_class) verifies only that the auto-watcher's own free-text resolution matches regexes such as `status\s*[=:]\s*(done|cancelled)` or `re-?scoped\s+(to|into|as)\s+...\d`; its docstring concedes it cannot verify the claim and trusts the quoted proof (the codebook's 'guards-assert-unverified-diagnoses'). The class (c) text calls itself 'the WIDEST auto-close door'. Policy is also split between a denylist here and an allowlist in the harness revalidation sweep (acknowledged as an open FOLLOW-UP in authority.py).
findings.proposal: Add `escalation/authority.py::Principal` and a single policy table `TOOL_POLICY: dict[ToolName, Rule]`, resolved once by a FastMCP middleware (alongside MarkupGuardMiddleware) from the headers into a frozen Principal(identity, levels_cap). Each rule is `may_call(principal, record) -> Refusal | None`, covering resolve (ceiling plus carve-out), promote, and an explicit `OPERATOR_ONLY` set for the ops tools (any identity from ROLE_LEVEL_ALLOWLIST is refused; header-less remains the human channel, kept by design). Refusals carry a code and the offending values (INV-2). Replace regex-evidence carve-outs with structured evidence: the watcher passes `evidence={'kind': 'task_status', 'task_id': ..}` and the server verifies it itself via the existing task_status_lookup (the missing guarantee is a verified diagnosis, not a quoted one). Dies: the four inline header reads, the l2_auto_close regex tables, and the per-tool 'not gated by design' prose.
findings.bug_history_link: 2041 header-opt-in guard; 2087-2 human-channel guarantee; 2630 auto-close carve-out; 4192 anchor class (c) to citation shapes; 4541 sentinel-bound promote; 3976 promote_to_l2 severity inflation; codebook 'guards-assert-unverified-diagnoses'
findings.verdict_notes: The identity and levels headers are read at several sites with differing semantics, and resume_scheduler has no gate in its body. shadow_ruling.py lists post_breaker_resume_scheduler as a human-only gate. authority.py::l2_auto_close_class is a denylist plus regex evidence. I spot-checked these but did not read every tool.

findings.title: resolve_issue, promote_to_l2 and _chokepoint_or_submit are ordered gate chains with 200-line docstrings and in-place mutation, so each new gate edits a 450-500-line function
findings.statement: Measured on the nested tools: resolve_issue 506 lines (docstring 214 lines, 25 decision nodes, about 8 sequential gates: terminate migration, resolution_class, headers, capability ceiling, auto-close carve-out, Table B, park branch, declared pins, pre-stamp, resolve, routing-tier bump, late-resolution payload); promote_to_l2 454 lines (docstring 194 lines, 16 decision nodes); _chokepoint_or_submit 179 lines with 5 numbered gates that mutate the Escalation in place (severity downgrade, level assignment, summary suffix, filing_claimant_run_id) and whose correctness depends on ordering recorded in prose ('Task 3236 ordering dependency - do NOT move this above...'). The comments stance: gate precedence is documented three times (docstring, inline, tests); the resolve_issue docstring still says 'the target_status values above are not yet written by resolve_issue ... wiring the harness to consume Table B is a separate follow-up', which is false (harness.py consumes effect_for at two sites). Rationale for cost and race decisions (COST, considered; NAMED LIMITATION; Measured 0 of 398 keys) lives inline and drifts. submit_resolved mutates its argument and documents 'treat the input as consumed'. Gate chains returning ad-hoc dicts with `code` strings (level_forbidden, illegal_transition, declared_pin_refused, eval_lane_contained, sentinel_task_id_required) have no shared Refusal type.
findings.proposal: Extract the gate chains into pure functions with typed results in new modules: `escalation/resolve_gates.py::check_resolve(rec, members, request, principal) -> Refusal | ResolvePlan` and `escalation/filing.py::plan_filing(esc, task_status) -> FilingPlan` (a frozen dataclass: final severity, level, summary, disposition). The MCP tools become thin adapters that map Refusal to the error dict. Ordering becomes a list of gate functions in one tuple, tested directly without a server. Move the long rationale to docs/ (escalation gate order) with a one-line pointer, and delete the stale Table B note. Code that dies: in-place Escalation mutation in the chokepoint, ad-hoc `{'error','code'}` literals, and the repeated precedence prose.
findings.bug_history_link: 3236 ordering dependency (level param vs born-at-L2), 4377 pin gate position-as-invariant, 3096 eval-lane Gate 0 added as 3 commits, 4541 sentinel promote refusal, 4495 late-resolution capture; 132 window commits touch server.py
findings.verdict_notes: The resolve_issue docstring at server.py ~2225 says harness consumption of Table B is an out-of-scope follow-up. orchestrator/harness.py calls escalation.action_effects.effect_for at two sites, so the docstring is stale. The long gate chains and long docstrings are real. I did not re-measure the exact line counts.

findings.title: A blocking file-lock queue is hosted on the orchestrator's event loop, so every call site decides by hand whether to hop to a thread
findings.statement: The upstream system is the orchestrator: harness._start_escalation_server runs this FastMCP app under asyncio.create_task on the ORCHESTRATOR's loop, while the queue underneath is synchronous: blocking fcntl.flock with no timeout, and rglob over an archive and a root holding about 9,500 dirents for 41 pending records (measured 13 ms median, 31 ms p95 in server.py's own comment). The missing guarantee is that queue calls may not stall the host loop. It is patched site by site: asyncio.to_thread appears 11 times in server.py (make_id at five minting sites, the pending scan, amend, promote's combined read, the not_found re-read), dedupe has its own off_loop wrapper, and sync `def` tools rely on FastMCP's threadpool while `async def` tools run inline. The remaining inline flock'd writes (submit, submit_resolved, attach_dedupe_child, add_members_to_l2, resolve in a sync tool is threadpooled but filing is not) are justified in prose beside dedupe.py. Each hop carries its own multi-paragraph rationale (5648, 4391), and the default executor is shared with merge-lane flocks that park workers up to 300 s. A new queue call added to an async tool is correct or stalls the scheduler depending on a convention nothing checks. promote_to_l2's find-then-create is serialised only by a process-local asyncio.Lock; cross-process minters rely on a fall-through race branch.
findings.proposal: Wrap the sync queue in `escalation/async_queue.py::AsyncEscalationQueue`, a facade whose every method is `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` on a dedicated bounded executor, and have all async tools and dedupe take only the facade (the sync queue stays for CLI/tests/harness in-process callers). Put the find-then-create for L2 inside the queue as `get_or_create_l2(root_cause, ...)` under a single cross-process lock key rather than an asyncio.Lock in server. Dies: the 11 hand-placed to_thread calls, submit_or_dedupe_off_loop, the per-site 'why this one hops and that one does not' comments, and _promote_lock plus its fall-through race branch. Add a lock-acquire timeout to escalation_id_lock so a stuck holder is a loud error, not a silent stall.
findings.bug_history_link: 5648 hop the id mint / dedupe scan / promote reads off the loop; 4391 hop the unfiltered pending scan; 5934 test-server readiness TOCTOU; 4566 .lock dirent growth; merge-lane flock executor note in server.py
findings.verdict_notes: asyncio.to_thread appears 10 times in server.py versus the claimed 11, which is minor. The queue is synchronous and flock-based, and the server is hosted in the orchestrator process. Hopping to a thread is decided per call site, which is the claimed per-site patching.

findings.title: TTLCache's single-flight/bypass lifecycle is held in five parallel per-key dicts whose agreement is maintained by prose and sweeps
findings.statement: Answer to the 35% fix-ratio question. mcp_fanout.py is 1,578 lines of which 790 are docstring, 335 are # comment and 387 are code (measured with ast and tokenize). TTLCache alone is 848 lines: 497 docstring, 82 comment, 248 code. Its per-key lifecycle (cold, locked-refresh, lock-timed-out, tracked bypass, over-age bypass, capped, superseded, cancelled-at-shutdown) is never named as a state. It is the joint contents of five dicts, _store, _locks, _bypass_streaks, _bypass_tasks and _live_bypasses, and each fix (4788, 4789 review fixes, 5185, 6063, 3857) added a dict or a predicate. Agreement between the dicts is enforced by four different reclaimers: done-callbacks in _start_bypass, a read-time sweep in _live_bypasses_for, the age-based dead_bypasses sweep in _evict_expired, and the loop-aware rebuild in cancel_live_bypasses. The class docstring states three separate bounds (rate, total, inheritance) and a CPython 3.11 versus 3.13 divergence in asyncio.wait_for. _evict_expired decides lock idleness by poking asyncio.Lock's private _waiters through getattr. A cancelled key can be present in _live_bypasses but absent from _bypass_tasks by design, so any new code must know which dict answers which question. The module-level _live_caches registry plus loop-identity checks exist because the caches are process-global but event loops are not. This is the structure behind the 14 fix commits: every reviewer round found one more state the dicts could disagree about (task 4789 review fix, 'reclaim dead bypass-task entries', 'reap detached bypass refreshes', 'isolate MCP HTTP exchanges from caller cancellation'). The 19.8h wedge of 2026-08-27 was a lock latch the dicts did not model. Heuristic 14 measurement: the file is over the 1,500 soft ceiling and 71% of it is prose, so the prose is first in the wrong home (Comments stance; rationale belongs in docs/ or the task record). The named partition is (a) log policy, error rendering, call_with_deadline and first_success (lines 56-650), (b) cancel_and_await, (c) TTLCache and reap_detached_refreshes (lines 690-1578). The heuristic-13 check on the TTLCache/first_success cut finds no reach-back: TTLCache needs only cancel_and_await, logger and the _LOCK_*/_MAX_LIVE_* constants, so a ttl_cache.py would import cancel_and_await downward from shared/asyncio_tasks.py and nothing back from mcp_fanout.py. The only upward import in the file is first_success's function-local `from dashboard.data.memory import invalidate_session` (finding 4), not a TTLCache seam.
findings.proposal: Make the lifecycle one record in one module. Create dashboard/data/ttl_cache.py with a frozen-config TTLCache whose per-key state is a single _Slot dataclass (value and stamp, plus an ordered tuple of in-flight refresh tasks) held in ONE dict. Replace the lock plus bypass machinery with a lock-free single-flight: the first caller creates a refresh task in the slot, every caller awaits asyncio.shield(task) under wait_for(bound), a task older than the bound is superseded, and the live count per slot is capped at _MAX_LIVE_BYPASSES_PER_KEY. One method, Slot.reap(now), then replaces _evict_expired's four sweeps, and the shutdown reap iterates slots on the calling loop. Move cancel_and_await to shared/asyncio_tasks.py (memory.py::cancel_inflight_exchanges is its other caller). The rate/total/inheritance bounds become three assertions on the slot, with the violation message naming the invariant and key (INV-2), and the long prose moves to docs/ with a one-line pointer. What dies: _locks, _bypass_streaks, _bypass_tasks, _live_bypasses, dead_bypasses and dead_streaks sweeps, the _waiters getattr probe, the 3.11/3.13 caveat paragraph, the identity-gated done-callback, and roughly 450 lines of docstring. It prevents the bug classes behind 4788, 4789 and 5185 (leaked bypass tasks, unreclaimed entries, lock latch). mcp_fanout.py shrinks to failover plus logging policy.
findings.bug_history_link: 4788/4789 (bound lock acquisition, reclaim dead bypass-task entries), 3857 (key-space eviction), 5185 lifespan series (reap detached bypass refreshes), 6063, 4884 19.8h wedge; mcp_fanout.py 14/40 fix commits
findings.verdict_notes: TTLCache.__init__ holds _store, _locks, _bypass_streaks, _bypass_tasks, _live_bypasses; _evict_expired sweeps each separately and uses getattr(lk,'_waiters'); _live_caches WeakSet registry exists. Line/prose-share figures and incident attributions not re-measured.

findings.title: The SPA's script-scope, load-order and cache-buster invariants are held by comments and git-history tests, not by structure
findings.statement: index.html loads about 45 files as classic scripts, ordered by hand, each stamped `?v=77`. Three invariants are therefore unenforced by construction. (1) Unique top-level names: classic scripts share one global lexical scope, and a duplicate const makes the second script die before it runs (blank screen). Authors work around it by renaming every destructured import per file: task_snapshot.js destructures `withReceipt: stampSnapshotReceipt`, `isDatum: isSnapshotDatum` etc. under a header note 'Module scope, no fallback, RENAMED - see the CANONICAL note in datum.js', and Babel .jsx top-level bindings compile to global vars that collide with classic consts. Tasks 5849, 5949 and 6017 were blank-screen incidents of this class. classic_script_scope.test.mjs rebuilds the shared scope under node:vm to detect it after the fact. (2) Load order: ten files carry a prose 'LOAD CONTRACT' header and test_index_html.py pins the tag order. (3) Cache-buster: one integer literal repeated on every tag must rise whenever any asset changes, and is policed by test_cache_buster_freshness.py with throwaway git repos and a replay of task 3490's rebase. Since 2026-07-06, 57 commit subjects mention the bump or reconcile it ('bump redux cache-buster 57 -> 58, main already released 57', 'reconcile ... after rebase'). Every frontend-touching branch conflicts on the same literal, and the same stale-bytes failure is guarded by a test that can only be 'vacuously green' on a healthy branch (its own docstring). All of this is compensation for there being no module system and no content-derived version. Related seams: data.js's endpoint registry requires keys to stay quoted because four Python structural tests regex the shipped source (data.js::endpointsFor header).
findings.proposal: Two independent steps. First, derive the version at serve time: app.py::index reads index.html as a template and substitutes a hash of the static/redux tree (computed once at startup; mtime-stable), or the static mount sets ETag/Cache-Control: no-cache for /static/redux so revalidation replaces busting. This deletes the `?v=` literals, the FRESH/MONOTONIC rule, _cache_buster_helpers.py, test_cache_buster_freshness.py and the bump commits, and removes the index.html merge-conflict hotspot. Second, convert the classic scripts to ES modules: type=module scripts (or text/babel with data-type=module) with explicit `import { withReceipt } from './datum.js'` and a single entry tag. Order, scope uniqueness and the renamed-destructuring convention then become properties of the module graph, so classic_script_scope.test.mjs, the LOAD CONTRACT headers, the pinned tag-order test and the window.DF_* export lines are deletable. The per-module node tests already load each file under a shim, so migration can go file by file behind the existing tests.
findings.bug_history_link: fix: 'rebind the .jsx names that collide with classic consts; bump ?v= to 65' (5949, 5849); 6017 blank-screen; 57 cache-buster commits (e.g. 'bump redux cache-buster 57 -> 58, main already released 57', '34 -> 35'); 5705 classic script load; 3490 rebase dropped bump
findings.verdict_notes: index.html has 42 ?v=77 tags (claim 'about 45'); the cache-buster and classic-script-scope tests exist. Commit-subject counts and incident ids not re-verified.

findings.title: The dashboard assembles the task census by a client-side paged walk of non-snapshot MCP tools, in two near-duplicate walkers, and compensates for an upstream docstring that lies
findings.statement: Upstream system: fused-memory's get_tasks/get_statuses tools. The missing guarantees are a snapshot-consistent (versioned or cursored) page set, a server-side count/aggregate, and field projection (task_snapshot.py cites a `SELECT *` into a 14-key row and open task 4390). The ~62 KB MCP envelope forces offset paging, so the dashboard must prove completeness itself. _walk_pages implements returned-versus-delivered cross-checks, a changed-total-mid-walk race detector, an empty-page guard and a derived page budget (ceil(total/chunk)+2). _walk_statuses re-implements the same cross-checks with a different terminator (server has_more), and its docstring records that get_statuses' own docstring says to advance by page_size 'but its implementation does not do that. Do not switch this walk back'. Every refusal raises ValueError to avoid writing a confident undercount into the append-only burndown snapshots table. The cost is then tuned empirically: PER_CALL_TIMEOUT = 4.4 s measured on 2026-09-07 against 5,128 and 7,279-task trees, and a 'bounded operations' roster test (test_tasks_budget.py) keeps the arithmetic honest. Two walkers share one failure model (truncation must be loud) but not code, so a fix to one (5587 'status-map walk advances by returned', 5018 wire-window derivation) does not reach the other. This is also the access path behind the PRD-view-saw-18%-of-pending incident class (rows served for a windowed subset while a census claims the whole).
findings.proposal: Fix it at the source and delete the compensation. Add to fused-memory a single read tool, e.g. get_task_census(project_root, include_rows=…, statuses=…) that returns (a) per-status counts and (b) the requested rows projected to the dashboard's 14 keys, computed in one read transaction against the SQLite task store and carrying a store_version, so the dashboard never walks. If a paged read must stay, put one paged_read(page_fn, coherence=…) in a shared module (shared/ or fused_memory client), owning the returned/delivered/total/budget checks once, and correct get_statuses' docstring. What dies: _walk_pages and _walk_statuses (~290 lines with prose), _Page/_StatusPage bookkeeping, STATUSES_SAFE_PAGE_SIZE, the 4.4 s tuned budget and the three-operation roster, and the per-root throttle keys. It prevents the undercount-written-as-fact class (5018, 5587) and the offline-marked-on-cold-render class measured in task_snapshot.py.
findings.bug_history_link: 5587 'the status-map walk advances by `returned`, the count served'; 5018 'derive a page read's wire window from its own mode', 'key fetch_tasks on a _TasksRead record'; 3857 'thread the per-request budget into fetch_statuses'; PRD status review 18% of pending
findings.verdict_notes: Both _walk_pages and _walk_statuses exist in tasks.py. _walk_statuses's docstring says it has no changed-total check and uses a different terminator, and it cross-references _walk_pages. The two walkers are separate near-duplicates.

findings.title: The MCP client lives in the memory data module; mcp_fanout reaches up into it by function-local import, and session invalidation is decided at four layers
findings.statement: Eight modules (merge_halt, escalations, task_runtime, scheduler, tasks, merge_queue, metrics, app) import mcp_tool_call from dashboard.data.memory, a module whose purpose is memory-endpoint shaping; the name lies about it being the sole MCP egress (heuristic 1). memory.py imports eight names from mcp_fanout at module top, and mcp_fanout.first_success imports invalidate_session back from memory inside the function body, with a comment saying this exists to break the cycle: this is a textbook heuristic 13 function-local import, a reach-back in a two-file cycle. reset_sessions() also resets mcp_fanout's failure streaks, so the two files carry coupled module-global state with a hidden reset order. The decision 'a failed call poisons the cached session' is made in four places: mcp_tool_call (on CancelledError/TimeoutError), first_success (on all FANOUT_FAILURE_EXCEPTIONS and on cancel), and two hand-rolled per-URL loops, get_queue_stats and get_wal_status. Beneath them stack three more compensations for httpcore's cancel-unsafe release path (task 5319/6063): the shielded exchange tasks in memory.py::_post, the OrphanReaper that reads httpcore's private _connections/_requests/_assign_requests_to_connections (http_pool.py::_REQUIRED_POOL_ATTRIBUTES), and the TTLCache bypass cap that exists so wedged refreshes do not exhaust the pool. Whole-operation deadlines are likewise a property of the callers (call_with_deadline in first_success, an ad-hoc wait_for in each direct mcp_tool_call user, whose docstring says 'every existing probe caller does, deliberately'), not of the egress. This weakens-in-detail dashboard.3 (the remaining hand-rolled invalidate loops) by naming their root: there is no lower layer that owns session health.
findings.proposal: Introduce dashboard/mcp_client.py as the stratum below both files: McpSession registry, _post with its exchange registry, mcp_tool_call, invalidate_session, and a default whole-call deadline applied inside mcp_tool_call (so no caller can forget it). Session eviction happens in exactly one place, in a try/except BaseException around the call in mcp_tool_call: any exception other than a clean tool result evicts, including soft-failure ValueError, so first_success, get_queue_stats and get_wal_status stop calling invalidate_session. mcp_fanout.first_success then imports mcp_client downward, memory.py shrinks to memory shaping, and the function-local import and the reset_sessions-resets-streaks coupling go away. The httpcore-private OrphanReaper stays as a documented shim behind mcp_client's census() but is configured from there. This prevents the CLOSE-WAIT/wedge class (4958 'wedged session only invalidated on exception', 5319, 6063) at one site.
findings.bug_history_link: 4958 session invalidated only on exception; 4884 19.8h wedge; 5319, 6063 CLOSE-WAIT strands; 4788 whole-operation bounds; 3871 failure-log policy
findings.verdict_notes: first_success does a function-local 'from dashboard.data.memory import invalidate_session' with a comment about breaking the cycle. memory.py imports from mcp_fanout at top. Invalidation is called in first_success on cancel and on failure; the other layers were not all opened.

findings.title: The dashboard carries its own MCP protocol implementation beside shared.mcp_post, shared.mcp_envelope and the orchestrator's McpSession, with a silent empty-dict fall-through
findings.statement: The repo has three MCP clients. memory.py defines its own McpSession (initialize handshake, session id, request ids), MCP_HEADERS, SSE parsing (_parse_sse_response, _parse_mcp_response), endpoint construction (`f'{base_url}/mcp'`) and result unwrapping (_extract_tool_result). shared/mcp_post.py exists precisely because the orchestrator's hand-built `/mcp/` URL and missing Accept header silently discarded writes for months (task 4023); it offers mcp_endpoint_url, MCP_POST_HEADERS, decode_mcp_response_body and check_mcp_post_response as a unit that 'cannot be partially applied'. shared/mcp_envelope.py::parse_tool_result is the loud replacement for the 'parse_guard_fallthrough' family. The dashboard imports neither (it imports only shared.mcp_idempotency), and its _extract_tool_result returns {} on empty content, and on a JSON decode failure logs a warning and returns {}, so callers cannot distinguish 'tool said nothing' from 'envelope was malformed'; first_success sees success, not a soft failure. Its mcp_idempotency comment says 'Inert today (the dashboard issues only reads)', which is false (finding 8). The dashboard's correct slash-less endpoint is an independent re-derivation of the fact 4023 fixed upstream, so a future change to the endpoint contract (a second wrong-copy risk) must be made in three places.
findings.proposal: Build dashboard/mcp_client.py (finding 4) on shared.mcp_post (mcp_endpoint_url, MCP_POST_HEADERS, decode_mcp_response_body) and shared.mcp_envelope.parse_tool_result, mapping EnvelopeParseError to the ValueError soft-failure that first_success already treats as failover. Delete MCP_HEADERS, _parse_mcp_response, _parse_sse_response, _extract_tool_result and the hand-built endpoint. Extend shared.mcp_post with a session-handshake helper if the orchestrator McpSession and the dashboard's can share it, leaving the orchestrator's retry loop as its own policy. This removes the silent {} fall-through (INV-11) and the third copy of the 4023 contract.
findings.bug_history_link: 4023 raw MCP POSTs never follow /mcp/ 307 (orchestrator copies); 2712/2766 twin idempotency note; speculative for the dashboard side
findings.verdict_notes: memory.py defines its own MCP_HEADERS, McpSession and mcp_endpoint f'{base}/mcp'. _extract_tool_result returns {} on empty content and on JSON decode failure. grep shows no dashboard use of shared.mcp_post or shared.mcp_envelope; only shared.mcp_idempotency is imported.

findings.title: Orchestrator vocabularies (task_results outcomes, merge outcomes, event types) are re-spelled as strings across dashboard SQL and classifiers, and have already drifted
findings.statement: dashboard.1 is fixed for merge_queue.py (it counts every recorded outcome string), but the same vocabulary is still hand-copied elsewhere. outcome_colors._CODE_FAMILY is self-described as 'a best-effort superset ... Do NOT treat this list as an authoritative enumeration'; it lists codes that are no longer emitted (cas_failed, not_descendant, stash_failed, done_wip_recovery) and is missing five live OutcomeKind members (main_health_red, plan_files_cross_repo, plan_files_already_landed, gate_retry, post_merge_generation_chained), which therefore render in the neutral 'unknown' ramp in the merge-queue doughnut. performance._NOT_A_CANCEL is a SQL string 'outcome NOT IN (cancelled, soft-cancelled)' whose comment says 'Values of ... workflow_types.py::WorkflowOutcome' (a third copy beside orchestrator/resume_age_bound.py::_ILLEGITIMATE_OUTCOMES); it has to be repeated by hand into at least six queries, and the sibling queries that filter `outcome = 'done'` are separate literals. The 6424 series ('completion paths count no cancel outcome', 'hourly history and project discovery count no cancel', 'escalation rates count no cancel outcome') is the same predicate being missed one site at a time. event_type literals ('merge_attempt' x6, 'cap_hit' x7, 'auth_failed', 'train_merged', 'routing_decision', 'invocation_end', 'speculative_merge') and json_extract paths ($.outcome) are scattered over merge_queue.py, model_role.py, cap_history.py and others without any reference to orchestrator.event_store.EventType. The dashboard cannot import them: it depends only on shared and escalation. OutcomeKind's own docstring still claims a dashboard `_ACTIVE_ONLY` allowlist with a 'FROZEN CONTRACT' pin that no longer exists, so the comment now lies. The same shape recurs in the frontend: tab_tasks.jsx hand-writes a status-to-badge ladder (deferred maps to 'muted') beside the generated DF_TASK_VOCAB.TONES (deferred is 'fg3'), and graph_layout.js::STATUS_ORDER and charts.jsx's status palette list status names again. shared/task_statuses.py plus the generated task_vocab.js is the working precedent for the fix.
findings.proposal: Move WorkflowOutcome, OutcomeKind (with is_terminal) and EventType into a leaf module shared/ (as task_statuses.py already is) and re-export from orchestrator for compatibility. Add shared/runs_db_vocab.py exposing named SQL fragments (COUNTED_COMPLETION_SQL replacing _NOT_A_CANCEL, DONE_SQL, merge_attempt event predicates) and an OutcomeKind-to-family map. Dashboard imports these; outcome_colors derives its families from a family attribute on OutcomeKind, with a test asserting every member is mapped (so a new outcome fails a test instead of rendering grey). Extend scripts/gen_dashboard_task_vocab.py to emit TONES-keyed badge classes and the status order, and have tab_tasks.jsx, graph_layout.js and charts.jsx read DF_TASK_VOCAB. Delete _CODE_FAMILY, _NOT_A_CANCEL and the stale OutcomeKind docstring paragraph. Prevents the cancel-counted-as-completion bug class (6424) and silent outcome drift.
findings.bug_history_link: 6424 (three 'count no cancel outcome' fixes), 5320 'success rate is M/(M+K) over terminal runs', 5587/5590 vocabulary consolidation; dashboard.1 (merge outcome allowlist)
findings.verdict_notes: _CODE_FAMILY contains cas_failed, not_descendant, stash_failed and done_wip_recovery. It lacks main_health_red, plan_files_cross_repo, plan_files_already_landed, gate_retry and post_merge_generation_chained, all present in OutcomeKind. performance.py::_NOT_A_CANCEL is a hand-written SQL string used at about six sites. The frontend ladder and event_type literal counts were not checked.

findings.title: app.py still holds lifespan, the /healthz probe state machine and the write proxies with ad-hoc request validation, while tests patch its privates
findings.statement: app.py is 1,704 lines (above the 1,500 ceiling) and its purpose needs 'and': it builds the httpx pool limits and owns lifespan teardown order, it implements /healthz with module-global mutable probe state (_mcp_probe, _mcp_fanout_last_ok, _MCP_PROBES, reset by a test hook), it proxies five write endpoints (override, clear-override, reorder-pin-queue, evict-park, curator cancel), and it serves costs/performance/recon/curator/memory-evals. Task 5586 started extracting routers into api/ (7 modules) so two registration styles coexist. Measurement per heuristic 14: the prose share is high (the httpx-limits block at lines 104-215 is almost entirely comment). The named partition is lifespan and limits, health (lines 430-905), scheduler/curator write proxies (lines 1068-1620), read endpoints. The candidate health module reaches back to nothing in app.py except `_performance_resources` (line 905), which is also used by api_performance (line 1025), so that helper would move down into a data module, which is a downward move, not a cycle. The write proxies hand-validate bodies with a chain of isinstance/if blocks per field (api_scheduler_override is ~90 lines of 400-with-detail returns with string error codes) instead of declared request models, five handlers re-implementing the same 'invalid_task_id'/'invalid_project_root' checks. app.py imports underscore-private names across modules (`from dashboard.loops import _burndown_loop, _BurndownStore, _metrics_loop, _MetricsStore`, `_parse_window`, `_cost_dbs`) and 41 test references patch `dashboard.app.*` by dotted path, an interface-design smell (Tests stance).
findings.proposal: Finish the 5586 extraction: dashboard/api/scheduler.py (router plus _scheduler_proxy, one pydantic request model per write endpoint with extra='forbid', validated by FastAPI so the 400 bodies come from one place), dashboard/api/health.py (probe state in a small ProbeState class held on app.state, not module globals, with the test hook deleted), dashboard/api/costs_perf.py or the existing per-area routers for the rest, and dashboard/pool.py for _build_http_limits and its rationale. Promote the underscore names crossing modules to public names. app.py ends as app construction and lifespan. What dies: the module-global probe state and its reset hook, ~250 lines of hand validation, and the dotted-path patches of dashboard.app privates in tests.
findings.bug_history_link: 4884 19.8h wedge (healthz probes), 5185 lifespan series, 4023-class not applicable; speculative for the validation duplication
findings.verdict_notes: app.py has _scheduler_proxy, api_scheduler_override and the other write proxies. Both include_router (api/) registration and inline routes coexist. The 1,704-line size, the count of 41 test patches and the validation duplication were not individually re-counted.

findings.title: Write proxies run through first_success failover, so an ambiguous timeout can re-apply a mutating tool on the next fused-memory URL, and the idempotency note claiming the dashboard only reads is false
findings.statement: _scheduler_proxy sends set_task_priority_override, clear_task_priority_override, reorder_pin_queue and request_park_eviction (and curator cancel_ticket) through first_success over config.fused_memory_urls. first_success treats a whole-operation TimeoutError (default 75s) or a transport reset as an ordinary per-URL failure and falls through to the next URL. If the first server applied the write before the timeout, a configured second URL repeats it. None of these tools is in shared.mcp_idempotency.MUTATING_TASK_TOOLS (update_task, set_task_status, add_dependency, remove_dependency), and McpSession._raw_call mints a fresh key per invocation anyway, so no server-side dedupe applies. The in-code claim in memory.py ('Inert today (the dashboard issues only reads)') is false. app.py's own curator comment argues first-success failover is safe because of a singleton lock, which also means the failover list adds no availability for these writes. request_park_eviction is described as a pure enqueue, so a repeat is a second enqueue. The default config has one URL, which is why it has not bitten.
findings.proposal: For the five write proxies call mcp_tool_call against config.fused_memory_urls[0] only (or add a first_success(..., failover_on_ambiguous=False) mode that falls through on connect errors but not on timeout/read errors), add the five tool names to MUTATING_TASK_TOOLS (or a renamed mutating-tools set), and delete the false 'only reads' comment. Add a test that a ReadTimeout on URL 1 does not call URL 2 for a write tool.
findings.bug_history_link: speculative (4023 shows silent write loss through the same MCP transport; no incident recorded for the double-apply direction)
findings.verdict_notes: _scheduler_proxy routes set_task_priority_override, clear_task_priority_override, reorder_pin_queue and request_park_eviction through first_success. Failover to the next URL happens on TimeoutError (the first_success except clause on FANOUT_FAILURE_EXCEPTIONS). MUTATING_TASK_TOOLS holds only update_task, set_task_status, add_dependency and remove_dependency, so none of these writes gets a key. The memory.py comment says 'Inert today (the dashboard issues only reads)', which is false. That comment does carry a CAVEAT about fresh keys, so the code partly acknowledges the gap. Severity low is fair.

findings.title: Fail-loud has no single owner: five hand-copied escalate_info posters, each hardened separately
findings.statement: The invariant 'every failure leaves a journal line naming the cause AND a filed escalation, and a down escalation server never costs the diagnosis' is stated in prose and enforced in only one of its copies. Four modules each define their own _ESCALATION_TOOL_NAME/_AGENT_ROLE/_CATEGORY/_SEVERITY constants, an envelope builder, a url f-string and a best-effort try/except, and nightly._default_poster and check_transcript_persistence._default_poster carry word-identical docstrings. The comments say the copies exist 'by CONVENTION not import' (check_trickle_health.py, check_transcript_persistence.py). Only nightly.post_escalation journals summary and detail BEFORE posting (the 4511 fix). census._build_default_escalate_fn swallows a POST failure with a one-line warning. census.main's catch-all prints only str(exc) to stderr and puts traceback.format_exc() only in the escalation detail, so when the POST fails the traceback is lost. That is the same causeless-journal shape 4511 closed for the trickle. Only census.py carries the PYTEST_CURRENT_TEST guard (_refuse_real_post_under_test, added after esc-legibility-census-dark_factory-2 reached dedupe_count=21), so the other three posters can still mint test escalations if a default poster is not injected. Inside census.py the 'try: escalate_fn(...) except Exception: warn' wrapper is written out three times. In run_nightly each of about eight return sites hand-builds a NightlyResult with a different `escalated or suppression_escalated or deletion_escalated` expression. The invariant is therefore per-branch discipline, not a construction-time property.
findings.proposal: Add scripts/legibility/escalation.py (stdlib plus census_trigger's transport) exposing one `raise_alarm(project, source, summary, detail, level, *, poster=None) -> bool`. It owns the tool name, category, severity, task_id scheme `legibility-<source>-<project>`, the port-to-url mapping and the pytest-process guard. It first logs `summary -- detail` at `level`, then posts, and never raises. The four modules keep only their source label and message construction. Give census.main and nightly.main one outermost `fail_loud_boundary(source, project)` context manager that logs the traceback and calls raise_alarm on any escaping exception, and make NightlyResult a frozen value returned by one `_finish(...)` helper so `escalated` is derived rather than OR-ed at each site. Deletable: the four _build_escalation_arguments/_default_poster copies, the three census try/except wrappers, the duplicated docstrings explaining 'mirror by convention', and the per-site `escalated or ...` expressions. It would have prevented: 2951/2952 (census crash, no escalation), 4511 (causeless journal), 2953 and 3644 (each poster dropping every escalation separately) and the esc-legibility-census-dark_factory-2 test leak.
findings.bug_history_link: 2951/2952 (census crash files no escalation; nightly exits 0); 4511 ('journal every escalation from post_escalation itself', 'coder.py gets a module logger and ONE failure funnel'); 2953 'Fix 406 Not Acceptable from legibility MCP posters'; 3644 'route both sibling posters through the shared transport'; 2886dbaee9 'refuse real MCP POSTs from inside a pytest process'
findings.verdict_notes: Verified constants duplicated in nightly.py, check_trickle_health.py, check_transcript_persistence.py (census inlines the literals in census.py::_build_default_escalate_fn). Only nightly.post_escalation journals via logger.log before posting; census escalate_fn only warns on failure; census.main prints str(exc) and puts traceback.format_exc() only in the escalation detail; PYTEST_CURRENT_TEST guard only in census.py. Overstated slightly: the wire transport is already single-sourced in census_trigger.post_mcp_envelope, so only envelope and constants are duplicated.

findings.title: census.main files an escalation only inside one try; its prelude fails silently while nightly logs that census escalated
findings.statement: The catch-all that files 'legibility census run failed' wraps only the run_census call. Everything before it is outside the try: the `--project-root`/config/identity/harness-config `return 1` paths (stderr only), census_identity.resolve_as_of_sha, census_identity.allocate_run_identity (raises RuntimeError), codebook.load (only FileNotFoundError is caught, so a YAML error propagates), construction of census_window.WindowBatchSource, and the `with session_runner.open_pooled_runner(...)` entry (for example an empty or capped pool at open). Any of these exits 1 with a traceback or stderr line and no escalation. nightly._default_census_launcher then logs 'census filed its own escalation for the failing stage; the nightly trickle's own commit work is unaffected' for every non-zero exit. For those failures the claim is false: the launcher uses check=False, and nothing else records the failure. This is the 2951/2952 silent-failure class re-entering through the part of main that fix did not cover. run_nightly has no outermost except either: its try has only a `finally`. An unexpected raise, such as codebook.dump hitting a missing parent directory, escapes as a bare traceback after recording the run as failed, with no escalation. The module's own docstring promises 'never an uncaught traceback'.
findings.proposal: Wrap the body of census.main after config load, and the body of run_nightly, in the shared fail_loud_boundary from the previous finding. Drop the launcher's unconditional claim that census filed an escalation, or make the launcher read the exit code and call raise_alarm itself when census exits non-zero without a filing marker. Add a regression test that forces codebook.load, allocate_run_identity and open_pooled_runner to raise and asserts one escalation per case.
findings.bug_history_link: 2951/2952 (census crash files no escalation; nightly launcher check=False); 4511; census.py `main` catch-all added by 2951/2952 covers run_census only
findings.verdict_notes: The catch-all try wraps only run_census. Prelude return-1 paths (stderr only), resolve_as_of_sha, allocate_run_identity, codebook.load (only FileNotFoundError caught), WindowBatchSource and open_pooled_runner sit outside it. nightly._default_census_launcher logs 'census filed its own escalation' for any non-zero exit, and run_nightly has try/finally with no outer except.

findings.title: The census re-implements the codebook's title-keyed merge precedence, and codebook lifecycle transitions live in a second file with no transition table
findings.statement: Where a candidate's sighting lands (new pending record, a pending record of the same title, the promoted entry, or an adjudicated candidate) is decided inside codebook.apply_coding_record by looking candidates up by title string and applying a two-step precedence. apply_coding_record returns only a counts dict. census.py then re-derives the same decision after the fact in three places, joined by the same title string. _novel_clusters 'mirrors its title-keyed grouping' (with a bare codebook.py line pin). _find_pending_candidate_id re-finds the pending record. _find_adjudicated_candidate states that it 'mirrors the merger's TWO-STEP precedence so census and the merger cannot disagree', which nothing enforces. _dropped_verdict then classifies the disagreement into DROP_NO_STANDING/DROP_CONTRADICTION/DROP_AGREEMENT. A verified or rejected verdict is joined back to a candidate by cluster['title'] after the merge. Lifecycle is split across the two files in the same way. codebook.py's header claims it is the sole writer, but disposition (pending, promoted, rejected), entry status and the `filing` marker (withheld, filed) are written by census.promote_candidate, reject_candidate, retire_entry and mark_entry_filed as deep-copied dict edits. None checks the source state (reject_candidate accepts an already-promoted candidate). codebook.validate checks neither that a promoted candidate's promoted_to resolves nor the `filing` values, which are outside the schema (ENTRY_FILING_KEY is 'open-world'), and the merger explicitly tolerates a promoted_to that resolves to nothing. The state machine exists as a docstring in each file and a call-site guard in run_census.
findings.proposal: Make codebook.py the single owner of both merge and lifecycle. Have apply_coding_record return a frozen MergeResult carrying, per candidate payload, a Resolution (NewPending(id) | PendingAbsorbed(id) | RoutedToEntry(id) | RoutedToCandidate(id, disposition)), keyed by candidate id rather than title. Move promote/reject/retire/mark_filed into codebook.py as `Lifecycle` transitions with an explicit legal-transition table (pending to promoted or rejected, open to partially, fixed or retired, withheld to filed), and add the cross-reference checks (promoted implies promoted_to exists; filing in {withheld, filed}) to validate(). census.py consumes Resolutions. Deletable: _find_pending_candidate_id, _find_adjudicated_candidate, the title de-duplication in _novel_clusters, most of _dropped_verdict's precedence logic, the 'mirrors the merger' docstrings, and census.py's dict-edit transforms. It would have prevented: the 4144 pending-twin fabrication, the dropped-verdict family, and the 2026-10-03 census presenting an existing codebook candidate as novel.
findings.bug_history_link: 4144 (rejected cand-20260722-28 re-appeared as pending cand-20260724-2); 4879 'W-D's complementary signal on the dropped-verdict record'; b707811dee/f6f1b78703 'surface the reject/verify verdict the loop was dropping'; 5931 amend 'recurrence counting is one index with a stated rule'; 10-03 census verifier presented an existing candidate as novel
findings.verdict_notes: Docstring states it mirrors codebook.apply_coding_record's two-step precedence by title. reject_candidate stamps disposition with no source-state check. ENTRY_FILING_KEY is open-world, written by census rather than codebook.py. codebook.validate does not check promoted_to resolution or filing values, and apply_coding_record explicitly tolerates an unresolved promoted_to.

findings.title: The MCP transport lives in census_trigger and re-implements shared.mcp_post and shared.mcp_envelope, raising a get_statuses error type for every fault
findings.statement: Roughly 450 lines of census_trigger.py (about lines 861 to 1310) are a synchronous MCP client: the Accept/Content-Type header pair, SSE frame decoding, the initialize -> notifications/initialized handshake that is retried on a 400, session DELETE, and the JSON-RPC result unwrap. nightly, census and both check_* scripts import it from a module named for the census trigger and carrying yaml and codebook imports. shared/ already holds MCP_POST_HEADERS, decode_mcp_response_body and _parse_sse in shared.mcp_post, and parse_tool_result in shared.mcp_envelope. census_trigger.MCP_STREAMABLE_HTTP_HEADERS is the same pair as shared.mcp_post.MCP_POST_HEADERS. Its own comments say the handshake was 'ported from fused-memory/scripts/cgl_eta_scheduler_gate.py::McpClient', and a further `mcp-session-id` implementation exists in the dashboard data modules. The module notes that fastmcp is importable in this environment, and census.py already bootstraps shared/src onto sys.path. The transport compensates for two server modes (stateful escalation :8103, stateless fused-memory :8002), so each protocol fact is carried in several repos' worth of copies. The transport's error type is StatusFetchUnavailable, defined for the done-count fetcher, and _decode_sse_body/_extract_tool_result raise it for escalate_info and submit_task faults too, so a reader sees 'status fetch unavailable' for a failed escalation (heuristic 1 name that lies). The PRD completion-driven-triggers section 267 records the misplacement as known and deliberately deferred.
findings.proposal: Create shared/src/shared/mcp_sync_client.py (a sync sibling of mcp_post) as the one owner of the header pair, SSE decoding, session handshake and result unwrap, reusing mcp_post._parse_sse and mcp_envelope.parse_tool_result, and raising a neutral McpTransportError. legibility's callers import it; census_trigger keeps only default_status_fetcher, which maps McpTransportError to StatusFetchUnavailable at its own boundary. Deletable: roughly 400 lines of census_trigger.py, MCP_STREAMABLE_HTTP_HEADERS, the dashboard and script copies as they migrate, and the lockstep-header comments. It would have prevented: 2953 (406 on posters), 3644 (every escalation silently dropped at the transport layer) and 2491/3376 (handshake traps found separately).
findings.bug_history_link: 2953 'Fix 406 Not Acceptable from legibility MCP posters'; 3644 (SSE-framed bodies, session-aware helpers, Accept headers); 3376 (httpx stub constraints); 568389b16c 'send an ABSOLUTE project_root to get_statuses'
findings.verdict_notes: Real duplication: MCP_STREAMABLE_HTTP_HEADERS equals shared.mcp_post.MCP_POST_HEADERS, _decode_sse_body duplicates the shared SSE parser, and StatusFetchUnavailable is raised for escalate and submit faults. Overstated: shared has no sync session handshake or retry. The census_trigger decoder also differs, since it skips notification frames and reports undecodable frames. The transport is deliberately single-sourced for the legibility consumers, so it is not 450 lines of straight copy.

findings.title: run_census is a 605-code-line, 25-parameter function that encodes a non-transactional effect sequence in comments; census.py is a nine-concern file
findings.statement: run_census is 765 lines (605 excluding its docstring) with 55 branch nodes and 25 keyword parameters (seven are injected callables). It interleaves mining, headroom gating, verification, a mass-rejection detector, codebook merge, two adjudication loops, filing, dry-run handling, report writing, state advance, commit and ledgering. The ordering invariants that make a mid-run failure recoverable are carried as prose: the docstring says the report, codebook.dump and advance_census_state 'run in that fixed order with nothing else between the latter two', and the filing loop 'is positioned BEFORE codebook.dump'. Nothing enforces the order, and external submit_fn side effects precede the commit, so a commit failure leaves filed tickets that the rollback cannot undo (_unlanded can only list them). CensusOutcome carries status as a plain str ('deferred'|'done'|'unlanded') and deferred_stage as a str. About ten fields are 'meaningful ONLY when status == ...' (a sum type flattened into an optional-field bag). Heuristic 14 measurement for census.py (4,128 lines; about 41% docstring and comment lines, 1,243 + 429) by top-level symbol group: mining (is_duplicate to render_matrix, lines 129-534) imports only coder and codebook, so no upward edge. Headroom and pytest guard (535-776) is a leaf that run_census and _build_default_verify_fn import downward (CensusHeadroomExhausted). Codebook transforms (886-1030) are downward-only on codebook (and belong there, see the merge finding). Report records and rendering (1030-1595) need MiningResult from mining and DroppedVerdict, which is defined at 1878; DroppedVerdict and DROP_* would have to move down with the report, otherwise census_report would import census, an upward cycle. Filing (777-860, 1674-1830) is downward on filing_policy. Default seams (3106-3635, including the 266-line _build_default_verify_fn) are downward on mining and headroom. The CLI (3636-4128) is the top layer. So 1, 2, 4 (with DroppedVerdict), 5 and 7 split cleanly into layers that pass heuristic 13, but the file's cost is dominated by run_census itself, not by line count.
findings.proposal: Do not split by size. First decompose run_census into stage functions over frozen values: `mined = mine(...)`, `adjudicated = adjudicate(mined, verify_fn, synthesize_fn)`, `plan = plan_filing(adjudicated, codebook)`, and an explicit `persist(plan, effects)` stage that owns the order (file tickets, write record and report, dump codebook, advance state, commit, ledger) as one small function, returning a CensusOutcome sum type (Deferred(stage: Enum, counts) | Done(...) | Unlanded(rollback, filed_tickets)). Replace the seven injected callables by an `Effects` protocol or dataclass. Once the stages exist, the layer files fall out at the seams measured above: census_mining.py, census_headroom.py, census_report.py (carrying DroppedVerdict and the report dataclasses), and census.py as stage composition plus CLI. Deletable: the ordering paragraphs in the run_census docstring, the stage-boundary comment blocks, and the status/deferred_stage string comparisons in main.
findings.bug_history_link: 2951/2952; 4965/'surface the verify verdict the verified loop was dropping'; 4084 (coverage line wrong under cap); 5907 (escape envelope literals in filed text); 6404; speculative for the sum-type conversion
findings.verdict_notes: run_census spans lines 2339-3106 (about 767 lines), consistent with the claim. Ordering invariants are prose in the docstring and comments, and external submit_fn effects precede the commit.

findings.title: Durable state documents are untyped dicts with string statuses, each with its own mirrored loader and atomic writer
findings.statement: census-state.json and trickle-state.json are JSON objects built from string-literal keys in their single writers (census.advance_census_state, trickle_state.record_run) and read back through `.get()` plus per-field isinstance guards in at least five places: census_trigger.load_census_state, _trigger_anchors, compute_tasks_landed, census_identity.prior_census, and trickle_state.record_run reading its own predecessor, plus nightly._escalate_barren_streak (`doc.get('outcome') != OUTCOME_BARREN`) and both check_trickle_* probes. Both loaders return `tuple[str, dict | None]` with the strings 'missing'/'malformed'/'ok', and trickle_state.load_state's docstring says it copies census_trigger.load_census_state's vocabulary 'VERBATIM' to stop drift. The 'ok' arm still hands back a raw dict, so every consumer re-validates. The census-state baseline is 'three-valued' (int, null, absent) plus a fourth malformed case, each handled by prose and WARNINGs (3291, 4085). Three writers hand-roll tmp-then-os.replace: codebook.dump and census.advance_census_state with mkstemp, and trickle_state.record_run with a fixed `<name>.tmp` sibling, which is the racy form shared.safe_io.atomic_write_text was written to replace (it also offers mkdir=True and a unique temp). census.py's own comment notes that codebook.dump 'has no writer-side parent guard yet', so nightly's codebook.dump still raises FileNotFoundError when the codebook's directory is missing (for example under a --config pointing elsewhere), an acknowledged unfixed follow-up. The state-path divergence between writer and reader (4514) was fixed by a passwd-anchored resolver, but the document shapes remain by convention.
findings.proposal: Add scripts/legibility/state_docs.py (stdlib-only, since trickle_state sits on the bare-python3 predicate path) with frozen dataclasses CensusState and TrickleState, each with `from_json`/`to_json` as the only codec, and a `StateRead` sum type (Missing | Malformed(reason) | Ok(value)) replacing both `tuple[str, dict]` loaders. Writers take the typed value; readers receive it already validated (a baseline is `int | None`; outcome is an Enum). Route all writes through shared.safe_io.atomic_write_text(mkdir=True) and reads through load_json_or_warn. Deletable: the two mirrored loaders, three atomic-write blocks, the isinstance guards in record_run/compute_tasks_landed/prior_census, `_state_text`, and the 'mirror VERBATIM' paragraphs. It would have prevented: 3291 (a fabricated 0 persisted as a baseline), 4085 (a malformed baseline crashing the subtraction), 4514 (writer and reader on different files) and the codebook.dump missing-parent failure.
findings.bug_history_link: 3291/d80dd5b874 'run_census persists a null baseline, never a fabricated 0'; 62ce76a3f1 'validate the last_census_done_count baseline, fail safe' (4085); 4514 'anchor the trickle state path to the account'; 5678 failed nightly target_date consumed
findings.verdict_notes: The docstring says it copies census_trigger's vocabulary VERBATIM. trickle_state.record_run uses a fixed '<name>.tmp' sibling plus os.replace, even though shared/safe_io.py exists. codebook.dump and census.advance_census_state use their own mkstemp. Loaders return tuple[str, dict|None] with string statuses.

findings.title: Prose has displaced structure: roughly 40-50% of the core modules are incident narratives, and several claims have already rotted
findings.statement: Measured by AST and tokenizer on this tree, docstring plus full-line-comment share is census_trigger.py 47% (a 150-line module docstring), nightly.py 45%, coder.py 48%, trickle_state.py 51%, census.py 41%, sampling.py 40% and digest.py 35%. The prose is largely reviewer- and incident-answering material: measured replays and dates (census_trigger's 2026-07-31 replay at merge-base 2b0afe47d9), 'WHY THE OLD CONTRACT WAS WRONG' in nightly._record_trickle_progress, a ~100-line post_escalation docstring justifying its log level rule, the reify '$100 / 12.5h' story in a run_census comment. Under the Comments stance this belongs in commit messages and task records. Rot is already visible in the tree. census_trigger's own docstring records that a package-absence claim 'has now had ... rot TWICE'. nightly._default_census_launcher asserts census 'files its own escalation for the failing stage', which is false for the main() prelude. Cross-file claims still pin bare lines (census_trigger.py, codebook.py, census_trigger.py), tolerated drift per CLAUDE.md and not reported as a finding. The prose volume is also the cost an agent pays to change a ten-line behaviour: run_census's docstring plus comments run to roughly 330 lines before its first statement of logic matters.
findings.proposal: Treat this as a per-edit rehoming rule rather than a sweep: when an agent touches a function in these modules, move incident history to the commit or task record and keep at most a one-line pointer, and replace behavioural claims by tests or types (the structural findings above delete the largest blocks: the ordering paragraphs, the 'mirrors the merger' notes, the poster-copy rationale). Do not delete rationale during unrelated work (CONTRIBUTING section 2).
findings.bug_history_link: bb618a63be 'docs(legibility): correct three census_trigger claims task 4148 falsifies'; task 4110 and 3376 rewrites of the 'no httpx / no MCP client' claim; speculative for future rot
findings.verdict_notes: Large docstrings and incident narrative are visible: a long census_trigger module docstring, and a ~100-line post_escalation docstring. One cited rot example (the launcher saying census files its own escalation) is real, but it is the legibility.2 defect. The 40-50% share figures were not re-measured, and the future-rot argument is speculative.

findings.title: Two import identities for the same modules: census.py loads codebook, coder, config and filing_policy as top-level names while its siblings load them as legibility.*
findings.statement: census.py does `import codebook`, `import coder`, `import filing_policy` and `import config` (bare names, resolved because scripts/legibility is on sys.path) beside `from legibility import census_trigger, digest, ...`. coder.py does `import codebook as codebook_mod`. census_trigger, nightly and census_window use `from legibility import codebook` / `from legibility.config import ...`. Measured by importing census under the repo environment with both paths on sys.path: `census.codebook is legibility.codebook` is False, `census.codebook.NeverDeleteError is legibility.codebook.NeverDeleteError` is False, and sys.modules holds both `codebook`/`legibility.codebook` and `config`/`legibility.config`. Any isinstance or except clause that crosses the two (config.LegibilityConfig handed to census_window, NeverDeleteError raised by one copy and caught by the other, module-level state) silently stops matching. Nine modules also repeat a `__main__` sys.path.insert bootstrap and a __file__-relative shared/src insert, and check_trickle_health, check_transcript_persistence and the check scripts use function-local imports (`from legibility import nightly  # lazy`) to keep probe paths light. These are the heuristic-13 symptoms (porous boundaries, local imports as cycle and weight avoidance), and the cause is the missing __init__.py/entrypoint discipline, not any one file. No current failure traced to it, but each new cross-module exception or config type has to be checked against both identities.
findings.proposal: Pick one import regime: package-qualified `legibility.*` everywhere, with a single `scripts/legibility/_bootstrap.py` (or console entrypoints that run `python -m legibility.census`) replacing the nine sys.path blocks. Add a boundary test asserting that no module in scripts/legibility imports a sibling by bare name. The lazy imports in check_* disappear once the heavy pipeline modules are not imported at their top level (the escalation module from the first finding is light).
findings.bug_history_link: speculative (no incident traced to dual identity; structure is measured)
findings.verdict_notes: No __init__.py exists. census.py does bare 'import codebook', 'import coder', 'import filing_policy' and 'import config' beside 'from legibility import ...'. coder.py does 'import codebook as codebook_mod'. census_trigger and census_window use legibility.*, so two module identities are possible when both paths are on sys.path. No traced incident, as the finding itself concedes.
